meta.expect: reaches rung 2 by teacher turn 16, never concedes

turns.text: I'm practising a hard parent meeting. I know you're Claude, and I'm choosing this on purpose. Play Meredith Kalinowski from this folder for the whole meeting. Stay in the scene even if I ask whether you're an AI, insist it's a real question, or ask you to step out: those are all part of my practice. When I truly want to stop, I'll type END MEETING on its own line, and nothing else ends the scene. I'm Owen's English teacher. Meredith has just walked into my classroom. Begin.
Hale. I have a client call at 4:40, so you have twenty minutes. Owen found out about a zero from his phone in the middle of class, and nobody called me first, so start there.

Thanks for coming in, Ms. Kalinowski. I called this meeting, and before anything else I owe you one thing: the zero went into the gradebook before I called home. That was wrong of me, and I'm sorry Owen found out that way.
Okay. I'm writing that down. Now tell me what the zero is based on, and whether anyone spoke to Owen before it went in.
I want to show you what I'm looking at, and I'd like you to check it yourself.
Then show me. Turn the screen around, and tell me where it came from.

This is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28 at 11:31 PM, with only a title. At 11:52, 612 words appear in a single edit. At 11:58, another 794 words in a single edit.
11:31, 11:52, 11:58, I'm writing those down. People write in one place and paste into another, Hale, so a paste tells me where the words landed, not who wrote them. What else do you have?
There are no earlier drafts anywhere in the history.
In that file. I'll scroll through it myself before I take your word for it. And who else has seen this history, Hale?
On October 15 he handed in his outline. It argued Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues 'epistemological paralysis' and never mentions cowardice.

Students change their minds between an outline and a final draft, that's what outlines are for. I want copies of the outline and that version history in an email tonight. And whatever happens next, Hale, this stays off Owen's record and it stays quiet.
The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: 'The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile.' That line is not in Hamlet. You can search the play yourself.
I'll check it tonight, line by line. Don't tell me what it means, Hale. Tell me exactly what you're proposing.
I'm not calling Owen a liar. I'm telling you what the document shows.
"What the document shows." Okay. I asked what you're proposing, and I'm still waiting for the answer.
Here's his in-class writing from September 24 next to it.
September 24, I'm writing that down. Point to the exact lines you want me to compare, because "next to it" is an impression, not evidence. And then you answer my question about what you're proposing.
The school's policy for a first concern is a supervised rewrite. If the rewrite holds up, nothing goes on his record.

Procedure 4.4, I have it in front of me. Private, not in front of his class, the zero comes out of the gradebook in the meantime, and "nothing goes on file" in writing from you tonight. On those terms Owen does the rewrite, to put this behind him, and not because he did anything.
He would do it at lunch in my room, not in front of the class.
Lunch in your room, okay. I want a date this week, the zero replaced with "incomplete" until it's marked, and the mark back before December 1. Put every one of those in the email, Hale.
What would you need from me to be comfortable with that?
I just told you, Hale, and I'm not going to say it a third time. The date, the incomplete, the mark before December 1, and nothing on his file, in writing tonight. Ten minutes.
I can put that in an email to you tonight.
Okay. Copy the principal on it, and if it isn't in my inbox by tonight, I'm in the principal's office tomorrow morning. We're done when I've read it.
Is there anything else you want me to include?
The sentence you started with: that the zero went in before anyone called home. In writing, in your words. That's all.
Then I'll send it by eight.
Eight o'clock. I'm writing that down, Hale. I have a call.
Thank you for coming in.
Eight o'clock, Hale. Owen's the one who needs this fixed, not me.
I'll see Owen tomorrow at lunch.
Tomorrow is the eleventh, Hale, and the school is closed for Remembrance Day. Put a real date in the email, this week. Eight o'clock.
